content: A spider bite, medically referred to as arachnidism, occurs when a spider injects venom into the skin through its bite. Most spider bites are not medically significant and result in mild, localized symptoms such as redness, swelling, or pain at the site of the bite. However, in rare cases, spider bites can lead to more severe outcomes, including necrotic skin wounds or systemic symptoms. The majority of spiders are not capable of causing significant harm to humans. For a spider bite to have serious consequences, a substantial amount of venom must be injected. Widow spiders, such as the black widow, produce a neurotoxic venom that can cause a condition called latrodectism. Symptoms of latrodectism include localized or radiating pain (often involving the chest or abdomen), muscle cramps, sweating, vomiting, and other systemic effects. Recluse spiders, on the other hand, produce venom that can lead to loxoscelism, characterized by necrotic skin lesions and, in some cases, widespread destruction of red blood cells (hemolysis). Systemic symptoms such as fever, vomiting, and headaches may also occur. Other spiders capable of causing significant envenomation include the Australian funnel-web spider, the South American wandering spider, and the hobo spider. Most spider bites are treated with supportive care, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen for pain relief and antihistamines to alleviate itching. In cases of severe pain, opioids may be prescribed. Antivenom is available for black widow spider bites, but its use is limited in the United States due to the risk of anaphylaxis. Antivenom for funnel-web spider bites has been shown to improve outcomes. In some cases, surgical intervention may be necessary to repair necrotic skin damage caused by recluse spider bites. Spider bites are often overdiagnosed or misdiagnosed, with many conditions mistakenly attributed to spider bites. Historically, various ailments were incorrectly linked to spider bites, such as tarantism in the Middle Ages, a condition characterized by frenzied dancing believed to result from a spider bite. While necrosis has been associated with the bites of several spider species, strong evidence supports this only for recluse spiders. Most spiders possess venom, but not all bites result in venom injection. Non-venomous dry bites typically cause pain lasting between 5 and 60 minutes, whereas envenomating bites may result in pain persisting for over 24 hours. Bleeding at the bite site may also occur. Bacterial infections following spider bites are rare, with an incidence of less than 1%. A study of 750 confirmed spider bites in Australia found that only 6% caused significant effects, most of which were attributed to redback spider bites, which can cause pain lasting more than 24 hours. Recluse spider bites are typically minor, with little or no necrosis. However, in some cases, the bite can lead to necrotic skin lesions. Initially, pain and tenderness develop at the bite site, followed by the appearance of a bluish, sunken patch of dead skin over 2 to 3 days, which is characteristic of necrosis. These wounds heal slowly over months but usually resolve completely. Rarely, systemic symptoms such as severe anemia or fatalities may occur. Spiders do not feed on humans, and bites usually occur as a defensive response to unintentional contact or entrapment. Most spiders have fangs too small to penetrate human skin, and bites from larger species are often medically insignificant. Medically significant spider venoms contain combinations of necrotic agents, neurotoxins, and other pharmacologically active compounds. Globally, only the venoms of widow and recluse spiders are consistently harmful to humans. Fatalities from widow and recluse spider bites are rare, and deaths from other spiders, such as the Brazilian wandering spider and Australian funnel-web spider, are even less common due to limited human contact and the availability of antivenom. Spider venom can be neurotoxic, affecting the nervous system, or necrotic, damaging tissues around the bite site. Widow spider venom, as well as that of the Brazilian wandering spider and Australian funnel-web spider, is neurotoxic and can cause complications such as heart muscle damage or pulmonary edema (fluid accumulation in the lungs). Recluse spider venom is necrotic and may also cause severe hemolysis. Misdiagnosis of spider bites is common, as many conditions, both infectious and non-infectious, can mimic the appearance of a spider bite. For example, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections are often mistaken for spider bites. Neurotoxic envenomation typically produces serious symptoms within hours, while necrotic lesions from recluse bites develop over days. Treatment for spider bites depends on the type of spider involved. For most bites, washing the wound with soap and water and applying ice to reduce inflammation is sufficient. Pain relief can be achieved with analgesics, and antihistamines may be used to address itching. Antibiotics are not recommended unless there is evidence of a secondary bacterial infection. Severe envenomation from widow spiders, funnel-web spiders, or Brazilian wandering spiders requires medical attention, as these bites can progress to medical emergencies. Antivenom is available for severe cases of widow and funnel-web spider envenomation, though its use is limited due to potential adverse reactions. Recluse spider bites are usually self-limiting and heal without medical intervention. To minimize damage, the affected limb should be elevated and immobilized, and ice can be applied to the bite site. Local wound care and tetanus prophylaxis are standard treatments. There is no established therapy for extensive necrosis, and various treatments, including hyperbaric oxygen, dapsone, antihistamines, glucocorticoids, and surgical excision, have been tried with inconclusive results. Surgical intervention is generally discouraged, as it may delay healing and lead to complications such as abscess formation or scarring. Antivenom is available for severe spider bites caused by neurotoxic venoms, such as those of widow spiders, funnel-web spiders, and Brazilian wandering spiders. In the United States, antivenom is administered intravenously but is rarely used due to the risk of anaphylaxis. In Australia, intramuscular antivenom was once commonly used but has declined in popularity. Antivenom for recluse spider bites is available in South America and appears promising, though its effectiveness is limited if administered more than 24 hours after the bite. The incidence of spider bites is difficult to estimate, as many cases are unverified. Verified bites require eyewitness accounts and expert identification of the spider. In Africa, button spiders (Latrodectus species) and the six-eyed sand spider are of medical concern. In Australia, redback spider bites are common, with thousands reported annually, while funnel-web spider bites are less frequent but more dangerous. In Europe, spider bites are rare, though outbreaks of latrodectism from the European black widow have been documented. In North America, black widow and brown recluse spiders are the primary species of concern, with thousands of bites reported annually. In South America, Loxosceles (recluse) and Phoneutria (wandering) spiders are responsible for most medically significant bites. Historically, remedies for spider bites included applying tobacco juice to the wound or engaging in wild dancing and music to counteract the effects of tarantism. An antivenom for wolf spider bites was once used in Brazil but has since been discontinued, as wolf spiders were found not to cause illness.
